prompt.brief: Design a distributed service that sorts datasets larger than one machine's memory and makes the sorted result available reliably to downstream consumers.
successSignals: Choose an external-sort pipeline with bounded partitions and spill files.
Explain partitioning, shuffle, skew handling, retries, and output commit semantics.
Separate durable input and output objects from ephemeral worker state.
Define validation, cleanup, observability, and cost controls.

functional: Accept a dataset and sort key or comparator.
Split, sort, shuffle, merge, and publish a sorted result.
Support CSV, JSONL, and binary records with schema validation.
Expose job status, progress, cancellation, retry, and result download APIs.
nonFunctional: Never require the complete dataset in one worker's memory.
Make task retries safe and publish outputs atomically only after validation.
Scale workers with input size while bounding shuffle amplification and hot partitions.
Preserve tenant isolation, encryption, retention, and auditability.
scaleAssumptions: Datasets range from 100 GB to 100 TB.
Input arrives in object storage and records have a stable sortable key.
A job may use thousands of workers and produce many output shards.
Most jobs are batch workloads with a completion SLO rather than interactive latency.

metrics.label: Input throughput
metrics.description: Aggregate scan throughput across workers for large jobs.

metrics.label: Shuffle amplification
metrics.description: Track bytes written and read during partition exchange.

metrics.label: Job completion
metrics.description: Target for a representative 10 TB sort with provisioned capacity.

metrics.label: Failed task retry rate
metrics.description: Detect bad partitions, transient storage errors, and skew.

entities.name: SortJob
entities.notes: The job record is the durable state machine and owns cancellation and retention.

entities.name: Partition
entities.notes: Partitions are immutable work units and can be recomputed from source data.

entities.name: TaskAttempt
entities.notes: Attempts use leases and fencing so a slow worker cannot commit over a newer attempt.

entities.name: OutputManifest
entities.notes: Consumers read the manifest only after the final atomic commit.

apis.contract: { inputUri, format, sortKeys, outputFormat, requestId } -> { jobId, state }
apis.notes: Validate ownership, schema, and quotas before creating an idempotent job.
Return stage-level progress and the last durable checkpoint.
Cancel queued work and fence running attempts before cleanup.
Authorize access and issue signed URLs only for committed manifests.

dataFlow.title: Register the sort job
dataFlow.description: The API validates the input manifest, comparator, tenant quota, and idempotency key, then writes a pending job.

dataFlow.title: Sample and partition
dataFlow.description: Workers scan keys or use range sampling to create balanced partition boundaries without loading all records in memory.

dataFlow.title: Spill sorted runs
dataFlow.description: Each mapper sorts bounded chunks in memory and writes checksummed run files to durable temporary storage.

dataFlow.title: Shuffle and merge
dataFlow.description: Partitioned runs are co-located with reducers, which perform streaming k-way merges and write immutable output shards.

dataFlow.title: Commit the output manifest
dataFlow.description: A validator checks shard ordering, counts, and checksums, then atomically marks one manifest committed and schedules cleanup.

architecture.title: External sort reference architecture
architecture.summary: A durable job coordinator schedules partition, sort, shuffle, and merge work over object storage while a manifest service publishes one validated result.

layers.label: Control plane
layers.description: Clients submit jobs and inspect progress.

layers.label: Data plane
layers.description: Workers stream source data and exchange immutable runs.

layers.label: Reliability plane
layers.description: Events, validation, cleanup, metrics, and audit operate independently.

keyPaths.label: Submit job
keyPaths.description: Client -> gateway -> coordinator -> durable job state.

keyPaths.label: Sort pipeline
keyPaths.description: Input objects -> partition workers -> shuffle runs -> reducers -> output objects.

keyPaths.label: Publish result
keyPaths.description: Reducer outputs -> validator -> committed manifest -> signed download.

components.label: Job API
components.description: Authenticates tenants, applies quotas, and validates requests.

components.label: Job coordinator
components.description: Owns state transitions, checkpoints, leases, and output commit.

components.label: Job metadata store
components.description: Stores jobs, partitions, task attempts, and manifests.

components.label: Object storage
components.description: Stores input, spill runs, output shards, and manifests.

components.label: Task scheduler
components.description: Places partition and merge tasks according to capacity and locality.

components.label: Partition sorters
components.description: Stream records, sort bounded runs, and spill them durably.

components.label: Shuffle index
components.description: Tracks partition ranges and run locations; data remains in object storage.

components.label: Merge reducers
components.description: Perform streaming k-way merges and write immutable output shards.

components.label: Job event stream
components.description: Publishes progress, failure, cancellation, and completion events.

components.label: Output validator
components.description: Checks ordering, counts, checksums, and manifest completeness.

components.label: Cleanup workers
components.description: Delete temporary runs after retention and recover abandoned jobs.

components.label: Sort observability
components.description: Tracks throughput, skew, shuffle, retries, stragglers, and storage cost.

connections.label: Job commands
connections.description: Create, inspect, cancel, and download requests.

connections.label: Validated job
connections.description: The coordinator owns the durable workflow.

connections.label: Job state
connections.description: State transitions and leases are conditional and fenced.

connections.label: Task plan
connections.description: The scheduler receives partition and merge work.

connections.label: Input and runs
connections.description: Workers stream input and write checksummed spill files.

connections.label: Partition tasks
connections.description: Leased attempts can be retried safely.

connections.label: Run locations
connections.description: Reducers discover immutable runs by partition.

connections.label: Commit decision
connections.description: Only one complete manifest is committed.

connections.label: Progress events
connections.description: Consumers update dashboards and cleanup schedules.

connections.label: Retention work
connections.description: Temporary data is removed after safe completion.

deepDives.title: Partition balance and skew
points: Use sampling or histograms to select range boundaries.
Split oversized partitions and use multiple reducers for hot ranges.
Track bytes and records, because equal record counts can hide very different sizes.

deepDives.title: Retries and speculative execution
points: Write attempt-specific immutable paths and commit through a conditional task record.
Fence stale workers with leases and attempt numbers.
Speculate only stragglers after accounting for storage and network contention.

deepDives.title: Output correctness
points: Validate adjacent shard boundaries and per-shard checksums.
Publish a manifest pointer atomically instead of exposing a partially written directory.
Keep failed output invisible and clean it after a grace period.

deepDives.title: Cost controls
points: Compress runs, colocate reducers with storage, and cap concurrent jobs per tenant.
Use lifecycle tiers for temporary data and delete it after the manifest is committed.
Expose bytes scanned, shuffled, written, and retried to callers.

tradeoffs.title: Range versus hash partitioning
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use sampled range partitioning when globally sorted output is required.
tradeoffs.caution: Skewed keys require adaptive splitting and can create boundary complexity.

tradeoffs.title: Managed engine versus custom workers
tradeoffs.recommendation: Prefer a managed distributed execution engine unless custom ordering or isolation requirements justify ownership.
tradeoffs.caution: A custom engine adds scheduler, recovery, and capacity responsibilities.

tradeoffs.title: Materialized output versus streaming
tradeoffs.recommendation: Materialize validated shards for repeatable batch consumption.
tradeoffs.caution: Materialization costs storage and delays first results compared with streaming.

commonMistakes: Loading the complete dataset into one process.
Using record counts instead of bytes to balance partitions.
Letting stale task attempts overwrite successful output.
Publishing a directory before all shards are validated.
Keeping spill data forever or ignoring shuffle cost.

followUps.question: What if one key owns half the dataset?
followUps.answer: Detect the hot range from sampling, split it into subranges using a secondary tie-breaker, and merge those subranges while preserving the total order.

followUps.question: How do you resume after coordinator failure?
followUps.answer: Persist the job state, partition manifests, leases, and committed attempts; reconstruct runnable work from the last durable checkpoint.

followUps.question: Can consumers read results while the job runs?
followUps.answer: Only expose explicitly marked complete shards with a snapshot boundary; otherwise consumers should use the final manifest for a consistent result.

followUps.question: How do you cancel safely?
followUps.answer: Fence new commits, stop scheduling, let workers checkpoint or abort, and retain source data until all attempts are accounted for.

rubric.description: The answer explains bounded memory, spill runs, partitioning, shuffle, and streaming merge.
Retries, leases, fencing, checksums, and atomic manifest publication are covered.
The design handles skew, stragglers, throughput, storage lifecycle, and tenant quotas.
Progress, cancellation, recovery, cleanup, and meaningful metrics are explicit.
